tier_reason: The bm_result.png screenshot of 'rake bm' shows real seconds xlsx_drone 10.633398, roo 20.406725, simple_xlsx_reader 25.493084, creek 28.266484, rubyXL 79.559665, produced by the public script test/benchmark/speed.rb in damian-m-g/xlsx_drone_rb; but it is a first-party run on 'my old notebook' with no CPU model, Ruby version or C build flags, so it stays C.

corrections.caveats: The benchmark lives in the Ruby binding repo (xlsx_drone_rb, which loads the C library through the ffi gem, gemspec 0.6.0) and measures the C library through Ruby FFI, not the C API itself; the baselines are pure-Ruby gems (roo, creek, rubyXL, simple_xlsx_reader), so this is native C against interpreted Ruby and says nothing about C or C++ xlsx readers such as xlsxio or OpenXLSX, or about openpyxl. Result is an undated screenshot from the author's own machine; the script test/benchmark/speed.rb and the 200,000-row file are in the repo, but CPU, OS, Ruby version, gem versions and C build flags are not stated, so tier C. Readers do different work: roo and xlsx_drone use random cell access by (row, column) while creek, rubyXL and simple_xlsx_reader iterate rows; rubyXL builds a full workbook object model; the script's own comment says simple_xlsx_reader cannot tell numbers from strings; each timed block also includes the gem's first require and the workbook open. No numeric comparison in the C repo README, CHANGELOG or issues. Category binary-schemas is a loose fit (spreadsheet file reader over zip and XML).

notes: Numbers and derived ratios (1.9x roo, 2.4x simple_xlsx_reader, 2.7x creek, 7.5x rubyXL) match the screenshot; record accurate. Shortcomings: C library measured only through a Ruby FFI binding against pure-Ruby gems (no C/C++ reader baseline), unstated hardware/Ruby/flags, readers doing different work, 21 stars, stale (last commit 2025-01-09).

tier_reason: Independent nativejson-benchmark suite: harness code public (src/tests/ujsontest.cpp against src/tests/nlohmanntest.cpp, build/premake5.lua), compiler stated (clang 7.0 64-bit on macOS), flags in premake5.lua at the sample's own commit a4a9f10 (2016-09-09: NDEBUG, optimize Full, -march=native) and CPU stated (Core i7-4980HQ); the CSV rows for 'ujson (C++)' and 'Nlohmann (C++11)' sum exactly to the record's 37.15 vs 72.48 ms parse, 24.86 vs 87.73 ms stringify, 29.28 vs 130.56 ms prettify and 3.02 vs 2.17 ms statistics.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: clang 7.0 64-bit on macOS as named in the README (in 2016 this must be Apple clang 7.x, since upstream clang 7.0 shipped in 2018; inference); build/premake5.lua at the sample's commit a4a9f10 (2016-09-09) sets release config -DNDEBUG, premake optimize "Full", and gmake buildoptions -march=native -Wall -Wextra, identical to the current file
corrections.caveats: Numbers come from the single 2016-09-09 sample run of nativejson-benchmark (by Milo Yip, RapidJSON's author, independent of ujson). At that commit the ujson submodule was pinned to 0d6259e (2015-04-12); the author's later commits of 2016-09-10 (escaped slash fix, int printing) and 2016-10-08 'Greatly reduce memory usage at the cost of slight reduction in parse speed' were never measured, although the benchmark's master now pins 65df934, so the current ujson parses somewhat slower than the sample shows. Baseline nlohmann/json is v2.0.3 (submodule c8d01fa), many releases behind the current library. ujson trails cJSON (24.67 ms), RapidJSON (7.93 ms) and ujson4c (8.95 ms) on parse and is slower than nlohmann on DOM traversal (Statistics 3.02 vs 2.17 ms); its parse memory is high (34.4 MB after parsing canada.json against nlohmann's 5.3 MB). Conformance in the same suite: parse validation 33/34 (fails pass01), parse double 66/66, parse string 9/9, roundtrip 18/27, against nlohmann 34/34, 66/66, 9/9, 23/27. Not compared against libstdc++, libc++ or MSVC STL (no std JSON exists). Project has no benchmark of its own; Bitbucket repo with no star count.

notes: Numbers verified row by row against the shared CSV (this project's 'ujson (C++)' row, not ujson4c). Flags confirmed at the sample commit, so the 'assumed to match' hedge is removed. Shortcomings: 2016 single run on a 2015 ujson snapshot that the author later slowed for memory, stale nlohmann v2.0.3 baseline, slower DOM traversal, high parse memory, 18/27 roundtrip conformance, abandoned since 2016-10-08.

tier_reason: Independent nativejson-benchmark suite: harness code public (src/tests/yajltest.cpp using yajl_tree_parse, same build/premake5.lua), clang 7.0 64-bit on macOS, flags confirmed at the sample's commit a4a9f10 (NDEBUG, optimize Full, -march=native), CPU Core i7-4980HQ; the 'YAJL (C)' and 'json-c (C)' rows sum to the record's 103.45 vs 134.55 ms parse, and every other number in the record matches the CSV.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: clang 7.0 64-bit on macOS as named in the README (in 2016 this must be Apple clang 7.x; inference); build/premake5.lua at the sample's commit a4a9f10 (2016-09-09) sets release config -DNDEBUG, premake optimize "Full", and gmake buildoptions -march=native -Wall -Wextra, identical to the current file
corrections.caveats: Mixed result, YAJL is mid-pack: its summed DOM parse time ranks 24th of the 40 parse rows in the CSV (rows include the strdup reference and three RapidJSON variants); it is slower than nlohmann v2.0.3 (72.48 ms), cJSON (24.67 ms), ujson4c (8.95 ms) and RapidJSON (7.93 ms, 13x faster), slower than json-c on twitter.json parse (8.28 vs 7.65 ms), and slower than json-c on stringify (78.64 vs 30.80 ms) and prettify (102.12 vs 49.26 ms). SAX round-trip 124.52 ms vs RapidJSON 18.14 ms and SAX statistics 47.35 vs 6.32 ms, so the README's hope to 'perform comparably to the fastest JSON parser out there' is not supported. Conformance in the same suite: parse validation 34/34, parse double 57/66, parse string 8/9, roundtrip 21/27. The sample is a single 2016-09-09 macOS run by RapidJSON's author with YAJL pinned at submodule 5e3a785 (2.1.0 per the README table) and json-c 0.12.1 (acbcc06). The repo ships its own perf/perftest.c (ChangeLog: 'a little in tree performance benchmark') and the ChangeLog cites a 20-35% parsing speedup over an older YAJL, but no comparison numbers against other libraries were found.

notes: Record accurate; only the rank wording (24th of 40 rows, which include strdup and RapidJSON variants) and the flags hedge were tightened. Shortcomings: mid-pack (only beats json-c, JsonCpp and Jansson on DOM parse; loses to json-c on stringify/prettify and twitter parse), 57/66 double conformance, single 2016 run, abandoned since 2015-09-24.
